newsitem.title: USA: Oklahoma bomb trial will not be delayed or moved.
newsitem.headline: Oklahoma bomb trial will not be delayed or moved.

text.p: The judge in the Oklahoma City bombing trial on Monday rejected defendant Timothy McVeigh's attempt to postpone his trial or move it to a remote site because of pre-trial publicity, saying a fair jury could be assembled.

U.S. District Judge Richard Matsch's decision paves the way for the trial to begin as planned on March 31. He rejected a claim by the defence that prejudicial news coverage would prevent McVeigh from getting a fair trial and also denied his request to dismiss the charges against him.

"I have full confidence that a fair-minded jury can and will be impaneled and that those selected will return a just verdict based on the law and evidence presented to them," Matsch wrote. He said an extensive jury selection process would be sufficient to counter news reports of purported confessions.

The move followed two published reports in the Dallas Morning News and Playboy Magazine that claimed McVeigh admitted planting the April 19, 1995, bomb at the Alfred P. Murrah federal building that killed 168 people and injured 500.

McVeigh's lawyers said in written arguments on Friday that the trial should be postponed or moved to Alaska, Hawaii, Vermont or the U.S. Virgin Islands because the published reports would have the effect of tainting a jury. But the judge rejected the view that the articles made a fair trial impossible.

"Past experience with jurors and a general awareness of public attitude about pre-trial publicity in criminal cases strongly suggest that these stories have had neither the wide exposure nor general acceptance that the defendant's lawyers presume," he wrote in his five-page opinion.

Matsch took note of the focus on the trial and growing media competition, saying there might be even more reports "with an increasing slant toward the sensational as the communicators compete for public attention before trial."
In fact, a third report claiming McVeigh's involvement in the bombing surfaced over the weekend in Newsweek magazine.
McVeigh's chief attorney Stephen Jones was not immediately available to comment, his office said.
Prosecutors on Friday said they opposed delaying the trial or moving the case. A trial date for co-defendant Terry Nichols, who is a close associate of McVeigh, has not yet been set.
